summary: One sign-in flow and one screen for both kinds of account: a kind-blind salt fetch, an identical client-side Argon2id derivation and HKDF split, an Auth Key on the wire, and a wrapper returned only after a vault owner's credential verifies, plus the stale-KDF upgrade, the idle lock, and the page's half of the vault epoch: how a page learns the vault was replaced elsewhere and closes it.

read.role: the Public group that /login, POST /api/auth/salt and POST /api/auth/login belong to, the Shared group that POST /api/auth/upgrade-kdf belongs to, the root path that resolves by kind, the variables that set every limit below, the pruning of the attempts table, and the gate's step 7 that answers vault-replaced, which sign-in is exempt from as a Public route
the import that replaces the epoch, and the page that posts the old epoch on the channel after it
owns the idle period and the session endpoints this flow's rules refer to
the credential row and envelope this flow reads
the input, button and progress conventions, the phone-width sizes, and the fact that the unauthenticated screens sit outside the shell
the one sign-in screen at one address, its two modes, the derivation wait, and the Replaced elsewhere state with its two wordings and what Rules says a replaced vault keeps
the Replaced since last open notice a sign-in that learns the vault was replaced lands on, with its two wordings

saltEndpoint.value: POST /api/auth/salt { username } returning { salt, kdf }, which is the password credential's params and nothing else. Two fields, and the response carries no field naming, implying or derivable into the account's kind

decoySalt.value: HMAC(server_secret, normalized_username) truncated to 16 bytes, plus the server's current default KDF envelope, for an unknown username. Deterministic, so it is stable across calls. Responses are identically shaped and constant-time

loginEndpoint.value: POST /api/auth/login { username, authKey } returning { kind, kdfStale } plus, for a vault owner only, wrappedDek, dekNonce and vaultEpoch. It sets the session cookie and writes last_login_at. An administrator's answer carries no vaultEpoch

wrapperAndEpochInOneTransaction.value: the wrapper and vaultEpoch are read inside the transaction that writes the session, so an import cannot land between them and sign-in never hands out one without the other. vaultEpoch equals the account's vault_epochs row, and after an import the next sign-in's equals the epoch the import returned

vaultEpochIsRequiredInTheAnswer.value: a vault owner's response without vaultEpoch is a failed login, as one without kind is, because a page without an epoch could send no vault request

vaultEpochInMemoryOnly.value: the page holds the epoch in memory, never in localStorage or sessionStorage. It survives a lock and the session ending, because the next sign-in compares it. Signing out discards it and a reload has none, so neither compares anything

vaultHeaderOnEveryRequest.value: once a page holds an epoch, every API request it sends carries it as X-Solvent-Vault: <epoch>, upgrade-kdf included. Sign-in, salt, logout and registration are Public and need none

pageLearnsReplacedFourWays.value: 1 a vault-replaced Conflict answering any request, handled by the API module before any caller sees it, so no screen's own Conflict handling (the version reload) ever runs on it. 2 a message on BroadcastChannel("solvent-vault") naming the epoch the page holds. 3 coming back into view: when an unlocked page's visibilitychange reports visible it sends one GET /api/records?type=profile through the API module and discards the body. 4 signing in to another epoch: the vaultEpoch a sign-in returns differs from the one the page held, on an unlock on a live session or a sign-in from the session-ran-out card

vaultChannel.value: BroadcastChannel("solvent-vault"). The message is the JSON object {"replaced":"<epoch>"}, the epoch that was replaced, and nothing else: no key, no new epoch, nothing decrypted. A page ignores any other message, one naming an epoch it does not hold, and every message while it holds no epoch. Every message a page posts has replaced as its only key

whoPostsOnTheChannel.value: a page that learns by Conflict or at sign-in posts {"replaced":"<the epoch it held>"} before discarding that epoch. A page that learned by message posts nothing, because every page on the channel received the same one. The restoring page posts the old epoch after an import. The channel reaches the pages of one browser profile and storage partition. A private window or another profile learns as another device does

learningByConflictOrMessage.value: the page 1 discards the Master Key, the DEK and every decrypted value as the idle lock does, 2 discards what a lock keeps (unsaved form input and every dialog that would come back after an unlock, a password field never counting) and closes every dialog, 3 discards the epoch it held so the unlock that follows compares nothing, 4 draws the unlock card in its Replaced elsewhere state in the wording for whether step 2 dropped anything. A locked page holding the named epoch does the same. A request in flight when the vault closes draws nothing when it answers. Unlocking from Replaced elsewhere opens the dashboard with no notice, not the view the page was on

learningAtSignIn.value: the page drops what a lock kept, opens the dashboard rather than the view it was on, and shows the Replaced since last open notice (ui/dashboard.md) in the wording for whether it dropped anything. A kept dialog counts as dropped input. The notice follows a lock, or a session that ended for its own reason while the page stayed open. It does not follow a sign-out or a reload, which discard the epoch so the next sign-in compares nothing

restoreIsTheOneExceptionToKeptInput.value: unsaved form input survives a lock, and a restore made elsewhere is the one exception, after which nothing typed survives. The product criterion states the exception, so qa and the reviewer assert the same rule

noticeWordingByDrop.value: two wordings per surface, chosen by whether the page dropped anything: dropped carries the critical icon, nothing dropped carries no icon. The exact copy is in the screen files

anotherDeviceMeetsReplacedElsewhere.value: import revokes no session, so a page elsewhere keeps a live session and its next request, or coming back into view, answers vault-replaced. It asks for the password only. It reaches the session-ran-out card only when its session ended for its own reason (expiry, log out everywhere, a password change), and then learns at sign-in

idleLockedPageElsewhere.value: a page on another device that is never used again closes no later than its idle lock, which discards everything but what a lock keeps, and signing in drops that too

lastLoginAtWriter.value: starting a session writes the account's last_login_at to the server clock, in the same transaction, and nothing else writes it. A sign-in, an unlock on a live session and a registration (register.md, Flow) all start a session this way, so an account that exists has one. Unlocking moves last_login_at and does not move issued_at. A wrong Auth Key, a rate-limited attempt and a locked-out attempt each leave it unchanged. Both kinds

decoyVerification.value: an unknown username still runs a full Argon2id verification against a fixed decoy hash and discards the result, so the endpoint does not answer in microseconds for accounts that do not exist

kindIsExplicit.value: kind is a returned field, not something the client infers from the presence of wrappedDek. A response arriving with kind absent is treated as a failed login rather than defaulting to either kind

kdfUpgradeComparesEpoch.value: a vault owner's upgrade-kdf request carries the epoch sign-in returned, and the server compares it after BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so an import landing between sign-in and upgrade is never overwritten by a wrapper around the old DEK. A replaced epoch answers Conflict {"refused":"vault-replaced"} and leaves credentials and dek_wrappers byte-identical. This Conflict is the one failed upgrade that closes the vault rather than leaving the session on the old parameters

atMostOneWrapper.value: the wrapper returned is the one belonging to the credential that just authenticated, never a list, and no field names, counts or describes any other credential. The lookup happens after verification, keyed on the credential id

clientDerivation.value: both halves always, Master Key and Auth Key, in a Web Worker, because the client does not yet know whether it will need the Master Key. Identical code path for both kinds

kdfParameters.value: Argon2id at 64 MiB memory, 3 iterations, parallelism 1, over a 128-bit salt, via the argon2id library, HKDF-split

serverSideAuthKeyHash.value: the Auth Key is stored hashed with Argon2id at modest server-side cost, starting point 64 MiB and 2 iterations. Defense in depth, not the primary work factor. Comparison is constant-time

signInWaitParity.value: the sign-in wait is the same for both kinds and must not be skipped for an administrator. The channel is wall-clock time at the keyboard, not response timing on the wire, and it is closed by the client doing the same work for everyone. What an administrator saves is everything after the verification and nothing before it

nothingPreAuthBranchesOnKind.value: the salt response, the client derivation, the Auth Key on the wire, the server-side Argon2id over it, the rate-limit keying and the lockout response are the same operations in the same order for both kinds

failedUnwrapIsAnAuthFailure.value: a failed DEK unwrap is treated as a wrong password with the same error, and nothing is logged, because the server never sees it. Do not silently continue with a dead key

kdfUpgradeEndpoint.value: POST /api/auth/upgrade-kdf { salt, kdf, authKey }, plus wrappedDek and dekNonce for a vault owner, against the authenticated session. In one transaction it replaces the password credential row and, for a vault owner, that credential's one dek_wrappers row. No other row changes

kdfUpgradeIsTheOnlyPath.value: this is the only path by which an account's KDF parameters are raised, and therefore the only way the Argon2id memory parameter is raised. Both kinds run it. The DEK does not change, so no vault record is re-encrypted, and a failed upgrade leaves the session running on the old parameters

kdfUpgradeDiscriminator.value: the server discriminates on the session's principal kind, not on which fields the client sent. A vault owner's request without a wrapper is a Bad Request and an administrator's with one is too

residualEnumerationLeak.value: a decoy always carries the server's current default envelope while a real account can carry a stale one, so an account not yet upgraded is distinguishable from a decoy. Accepted, not closed. It leaks existence, never kind. Do not write a test asserting a stale-envelope account is indistinguishable

idleLock.value: for a vault owner, after the configured idle period the client discards the Master Key, the DEK and every decrypted value derived from them, meaning the whole in-memory model, rendered figures, chart series and any cached plaintext, then shows a re-unlock prompt. The server session may still be valid, and unlocking re-derives the keys and re-decrypts the vault from scratch

idleLockException.value: unsaved form input the user typed survives the lock, scoped to the open form. Nothing else decrypted is exempt. The same rule covers the manual lock button and a session expiring mid-request. A replaced vault is the one lock it does not cover: the held input goes

pageLeftWhileUnlocked.value: the vault shell page is served with Cache-Control: no-store, and the client locks on pagehide, discarding the keys and the decrypted state the way the idle lock does, so Back shows the unlock card and no vault data

noIdleRuleForAdministrator.value: nothing is decrypted, so there is nothing for a lock to take away. An administrator session is bounded by the absolute expiry and by signing out

sessionLifetime.value: the server-side session expires 12 hours after its issued_at, absolute and not sliding, for both kinds. issued_at is the sign-in that created the row and no later unlock moves it

sessionOnSignIn.value: a successful POST /api/auth/login always issues a new random token. A live same-account session row is updated in place with the new token_hash, keeping id and issued_at, and the old token stops working at once. No live session (no cookie, bad signature, token matching no row, expired row) creates a new row. A live session of another account is deleted and a new row created. In every case the signing-in account's expired rows are deleted in the same transaction. Live means not past the absolute expiry

failedLoginWritesNoSession.value: a failed login, a rate-limited or locked-out one included, writes no session row and leaves the carried session working

noUnlockEndpoint.value: the unlock prompt after an idle lock, the lock button or a refresh calls POST /api/auth/login, which is the one place that returns the wrapper, runs the decoy verification and is rate limited. The branch on the carried session runs only after the Auth Key verified

rateLimitScope.value: guards /api/auth/salt and /api/auth/login. Both check every limit before doing any work, and a request any one refuses gets Too Many Requests with the same body and headers whether or not the username exists and whatever its kind

perUsernameLimit.value: 10 failed sign-ins within 15 minutes throttle the username until the oldest leaves the window. 20 within 60 minutes lock it for 15 minutes from the failure that tripped the lock. Variables LOGIN_ATTEMPTS_PER_ACCOUNT, LOGIN_ACCOUNT_WINDOW_MINUTES, LOGIN_LOCKOUT_THRESHOLD, LOGIN_LOCKOUT_WINDOW_MINUTES, LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MINUTES

perAddressLimit.value: 30 failed sign-ins from one client address within 15 minutes lock that address for 15 minutes from the failure that tripped the lock. The lock refuses every username from that address, administrators included, on both endpoints. Variables LOGIN_FAILURES_PER_ADDRESS, LOGIN_ADDRESS_WINDOW_MINUTES, LOGIN_ADDRESS_LOCK_MINUTES. There is no per-IP request limit: LOGIN_REQUESTS_PER_IP_HOUR refuses to start whenever set (app-shell contract)

limitsAreOperatorConfig.value: every limit and the concurrency cap is operator config with the stated default, and the address window and address lock also set how long an address key is kept. Tests assert behaviour at the configured value: the limit engages, the lock holds and ends on time, and the response does not reveal whether the account exists

whatCountsAsAFailure.value: a failed sign-in is a /api/auth/login whose verification, real or decoy, did not match. Not the salt fetch, not a Bad Request, not a request the concurrency cap or a limit turned away. A wrong Auth Key for a real or an unknown username writes one failure row in the username's bucket and one in the address's

refusedRequestWritesNoRow.value: a refused request writes no attempts row, so a lock runs from the failure that tripped it and retrying during a throttle or a lock never lengthens it. This holds for a limit, a salt fetch that answers OK, a Bad Request and a sign-in the concurrency cap turned away, on either endpoint

successDeletesUsernameFailures.value: a successful sign-in deletes its username's login: and login-lock: rows and none of its address's, because one valid account would otherwise reset its address's budget between guesses

freshLockWhileWindowHolds.value: a failure while the window still holds the threshold trips a fresh lock, so a lock shorter than its window can follow another at once

attemptsTable.value: (bucket, outcome, at), indexed on (bucket, at), outcome one of request and failure, at from the server clock. SQLite rather than process memory, so every gunicorn worker shares one budget and a restart hands an attacker no fresh one

value.login:<normalized username>: one row per failed sign-in, failure, deleted once older than the longer of the per-username throttle window and lock window
value.login-lock:<normalized username>: one row per lock tripped, failure, deleted once older than the per-username lock
value.address:<address key>: one row per failed sign-in, failure, deleted once older than the address window
value.address-lock:<address key>: one row per lock tripped, failure, deleted once older than the address lock

lockIsItsOwnRow.value: a lock, per-username or per-address, is its own row, login-lock: or address-lock:, written in the transaction of the failure that tripped it and holding while its at is within the lock's length. Nothing else decides whether a lock holds, because a lock derived from the failures in its window would lift early once the earliest of them aged out. The throttle and the rates and export limits are derived from the rows in their windows. No bucket holds an address in any other form

lockRowWrittenOncePerTrip.value: the failure that trips a per-username lock writes exactly one login-lock: row and the one that trips an address lock exactly one address-lock: row, each in the same transaction as the failure's own rows. A failure that trips neither writes neither

usernameLockScenario.value: at the default limits, with the per-address limits out of reach and the clock stubbed: 10 wrong Auth Keys at 0:00, 9 at 15:01 and the 20th at 59:00. The username's correct Auth Key gets Too Many Requests (429) at 60:01, after the 0:00 failures left the lock window, and at 74:00, and signs in at 74:01

addressKey.value: the first 16 bytes, as lowercase hex, of HMAC-SHA256 under the address subkey over the canonical address in ASCII. The subkey is HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869) with SECRET_KEY's UTF-8 bytes as input keying material, no salt (32 zero bytes), info 'solvent attempts address v1' in ASCII, and 32 bytes of output. HKDF is the standard library's hmac in RFC 5869's two steps, checked against Test Case 1, not a dependency. An unkeyed hash is rejected

canonicalAddress.value: an IPv4 address in dotted decimal. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address as its IPv4 address. Any other IPv6 address as its /64 network in Python's compressed form (2001:db8:1:2::/64). A value that parses as neither is the literal 'invalid', one shared key

clientAddressSource.value: the TCP peer's address, unless TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is N > 0, when Werkzeug's ProxyFix(x_for=N) takes the Nth entry from the right of X-Forwarded-For. Only x_for is set. With N = 0, the first request in a process carrying X-Forwarded-For logs config.proxy_header_ignored once at WARNING, naming TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS and no header value

noAddressKept.value: the address is used for the address limit and nothing else. No table, response or log line carries a client address, a user agent or a referrer. The attempts table's address keys are the one trace a connection leaves, and every SQLite connection sets PRAGMA secure_delete = ON

attemptsRetention.value: a row is deleted once older than the longest window any check reads its bucket over (login: the longer of the per-username throttle window and lock window, login-lock: the per-username lock, address: the address window, address-lock: the address lock). Deletion runs at process start and once a minute in each serving process (app-shell contract), so at the defaults a failed connection's trace is gone within about a quarter of an hour

concurrencyCap.value: Auth Key verifications run behind a concurrency limit, default 4, so peak Argon2id memory is bounded. A verification over it waits at most 10 seconds for a slot by default, then answers with the ordinary throttle response

lockoutAlerting.value: each lock logs exactly one line at WARNING when it trips, never on the requests it refuses: 'auth.lockout scope=username username=<name> lock_minutes=<n>' or 'auth.lockout scope=address lock_minutes=<n>'. <name> is the normalized username as a JSON string, so a crafted username cannot forge a line. The address line carries no address and no address key. There is no email or push path

lockedOutOrOverLimit.condition: a rate limit engaged, a lock included, or the concurrency cap's wait ran out. Same body and headers for every username and kind, so the response must not reveal whether the account exists (spec/architecture.md#application-hardening, spec/features/login.md#edge-cases). A correct password during a lock gets it too

credentialVerifiesWithNoWrapper.condition: a vault owner whose credential verifies but who has no wrapper. Counted as no failure, because the password was right (spec/features/login.md#edge-cases)

sessionExpiredMidRequest.condition: the status alone is the signal, with no code in the body. The client prompts for re-unlock rather than discarding unsaved input, unless that sign-in finds the vault replaced (spec/features/login.md#edge-cases)

vaultReplaced.condition: a vault owner's request, upgrade-kdf included, carrying an epoch that is not the vault's. The body is {"refused":"vault-replaced"} and the page closes the vault (spec/features/login.md#a-vault-replaced-elsewhere)

upgradeKdfFieldMismatch.condition: a wrapper from an administrator session, or none from a vault owner session (spec/features/login.md#stale-kdf-upgrade)

fixtures: a seeded vault owner, a seeded administrator and an unknown username, all three at current KDF parameters, for the three-way salt and login comparisons
browser-side timing capture from form submission to the Auth Key leaving the browser, for the wall-clock parity assertion
an account of each kind stored at a KDF envelope below the server default, for the upgrade path
a record written before an upgrade, to prove the DEK is unchanged by decrypting it afterwards
a server default Argon2id memory parameter that can be raised in the test, for the live-upgrade-path assertion
a stubbed /api/auth/upgrade-kdf returning Server Error, for the keep-signed-in assertion
a populated in-memory model, inspectable after an idle lock, for the assertion that no decrypted account name, value or snapshot remains reachable
a full before-and-after snapshot of principals, credentials and dek_wrappers, for the assertion that an upgrade writes one credential row and at most its own wrapper

one client carrying its cookie across sign-ins, plus a second account's live cookie, a sessions row past the absolute expiry, and a second live row of the same account, for the sessions-row assertions
a clock that can move 11 and 12 hours past the first sign-in, for the unlock-does-not-move-issued_at assertion
a stubbed server clock, for the last_login_at assertions on a sign-in and on an unlock, for an account of each kind
a wrong Auth Key, a rate-limited attempt and a locked-out attempt against an account with a known last_login_at, for the unchanged assertion
a stubbed clock and the attempts table readable row for row, for the lock-ends-on-time, retry-writes-nothing and failure-row assertions
operator config that puts the per-username limits out of reach, for the per-address assertions, and one that puts the per-address limit out of reach, for the per-username ones
failed sign-ins from 203.0.113.7 and from 2001:db8:1:2::5 set as the WSGI REMOTE_ADDR, for the no-plaintext-address scan of every table, the database file's bytes and every captured log line
a test SECRET_KEY that can be changed, for the address-key derivation assertion
address pairs 2001:db8:1:2::5 and ::6, 2001:db8:1:3::5, ::ffff:203.0.113.7 and 203.0.113.7, and two unparseable addresses, for the canonical-address assertion
RFC 5869 Test Case 1, for the HKDF function
TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS at 0 and at 1, with peers whose X-Forwarded-For entries differ, for the client-address assertions, and log capture for config.proxy_header_ignored
log capture at WARNING, with a username containing a newline and a quote, for the auth.lockout assertions
a stubbed concurrency cap whose wait runs out, for the no-row assertion
wrong Auth Keys applied on the schedule 10 at 0:00, 9 at 15:01, 1 at 59:00, with the per-address limits out of reach and the clock stubbed, for the username-lock-lasts-its-full-length assertion

two pages of one browser context unlocked on one vault, one with a holding form open and a name typed and one showing only the dashboard, plus a real import from the first, for the Two pages, one browser assertions and the nothing-dropped wording
a BroadcastChannel stubbed so no message arrives, for the Conflict-only path and its posted message

a page in a second browser context with its own session, hidden through a restore made in the first and then made visible, with the requests it sends captured, for the coming-back-into-view assertion and the session row still existing

a page locked by the idle period in a second context through a restore, once with a form's input held, once with a dialog kept and nothing typed, once with nothing kept, for the three sign-in wordings and the posted message

a second context that logs out everywhere, signs in again and restores, while the first holds typed input, for the session-ran-out card and the sign-in that finds the vault replaced; and the same without a restore in between

a captured channel that every page of the context posts to, plus messages naming an epoch the page does not hold, of another shape, and sent to a page holding no epoch, for the ignore assertions and the only-key-is-replaced assertion
a stale epoch from before an import and a vault owner session, for the upgrade-kdf Conflict and the byte-identical credentials and dek_wrappers rows
localStorage and sessionStorage dumped at every step of the sign-in, upgrade, lock, unlock and restore flow, for the no-epoch-stored assertion
focus: the administrator sign-in wait must be measured in the browser, from form submission to the Auth Key leaving it, and compared against a vault owner's and an unknown username's. This is the criterion the whole two-kind design turns on and it is invisible to every server-side timing test, because the channel is wall-clock time at the keyboard. It is also the test that fails if somebody later makes the administrator path skip the derivation, which is the obvious optimization

the salt response must be compared three ways, administrator against vault owner against unknown, over the endpoint's full response shape and field set, not only its two documented fields. An added field is the failure mode, and it breaks this silently
the client derivation must be compared as a code path taken, not only as an output. Two paths that produce the same bytes today can diverge in cost tomorrow, which is the leak
do not write a test asserting that a stale-envelope account is indistinguishable from a decoy. The spec states outright that it is not, and a green test there would assert something untrue

the idle-lock criterion must be asserted against the in-memory model, not only against the key handles. Dropping the keys and leaving the decrypted model in place passes any test that checks for a Master Key and fails the threat the lock exists for
re-unlocking must be shown to refetch and re-decrypt rather than restore a model kept across the lock. A cached model that is simply re-exposed looks identical from the outside

the upgrade must be shown to write exactly the password credential row and, for a vault owner, that credential's wrapper, by comparing every other row of principals, credentials and dek_wrappers before and after

an administrator's verifier must be shown to be a hash over the HKDF half and not over the raw Argon2id output, by deriving both in a test and checking which one verifies. Both produce a working login, so only this comparison tells them apart

the sessions assertions must compare rows, not cookies alone: after sign-in, sign-in, a failed attempt and sign-in again, exactly one row remains with the first id and issued_at, every replaced cookie answers Unauthorized, and the cookie carried into the failed attempt still worked afterwards. A rotation that inserts a row and leaves the old one passes any test that only checks the new cookie

unlock 11 hours after sign-in must be shown to leave a session that answers Unauthorized at 12 hours from the first sign-in. An implementation that resets issued_at on unlock passes everything else and makes the limit sliding

last_login_at must be asserted for both kinds with the clock stubbed, on a sign-in and on an unlock of a live session, with issued_at unchanged by the unlock, and must be shown unchanged after a wrong Auth Key, a rate-limited attempt and a locked-out attempt. A write that happens before verification, or that only runs on the first sign-in, passes a test over one happy path
a sign-in with no cookie must leave the account's other live rows untouched, and must delete only the signing-in account's expired rows, asserted against the table
no key material may be written to localStorage or sessionStorage at any point, asserted over the whole flow including the upgrade and the re-unlock, not only the first sign-in

the lock must be shown to end on time despite retries: trip an address lock, retry every minute with a salt fetch, a wrong Auth Key and the administrator's correct Auth Key, each Too Many Requests, compare the attempts row count before and after, then sign in at the lock's length plus one second. A limiter that writes a row per refused request passes every test that does not retry during the lock, and the lock never ends. Repeat for a per-username lock

a request refused by any limit, on either endpoint, must leave the attempts table row for row as it was, and so must a salt fetch that answers OK, a Bad Request and a sign-in the concurrency cap turned away. Asserting the count of failures alone misses a request row

the per-address lock must be asserted with the per-username limits out of reach and failures spread over unknown usernames, then the administrator's username, a vault owner's and an unknown one each answer Too Many Requests byte-identical, while a different address signs the administrator in. A per-username test cannot show that one address's guesses lock a name it never tried
the refusal for a throttle, a username lock and an address lock must each be byte-identical to the refusal for a nonexistent username pushed over the same limit, body and headers

no plaintext address may be found anywhere: every table, the database file's bytes (secure_delete is what keeps a deleted row's address out of the free pages) and every captured log line, for an IPv4 and an IPv6 address and the /64 network. A column check alone passes while the file holds the bytes

the address key must be computed by the test from the spec's derivation with the test's SECRET_KEY and compared with the bucket's key, and must change when SECRET_KEY does. Asserting only that a key looks like hex passes an unkeyed hash, which reverses in seconds

the proxy assertions need both hop counts: with 0, failures from one peer carrying a different X-Forwarded-For each time lock that peer, and with 1 requests whose last entry differs count apart while a client-written entry left of the proxy changes nothing. A test at one hop count passes a header that is trusted either always or never

a lock must log exactly one auth.lockout line and the requests it refuses none, the address line must carry no address and no address key, and a crafted username must stay on one line as a JSON string. A line logged per refused request, or an unescaped name, passes a test that only looks for the line

a successful sign-in must delete its username's login: and login-lock: rows and leave the address's address: and address-lock: rows, asserted against the table. An implementation that clears both lets one valid account reset its address's budget between guesses, and one that clears login: alone leaves a lock row holding

the username lock must be asserted on the schedule 10 failures at 0:00, 9 at 15:01 and the 20th at 59:00, with Too Many Requests at 60:01 and 74:00 and a sign-in at 74:01. A lock derived from the failures in its window lifts at 60:01 when the 0:00 failures age out, and passes any test whose failures arrive together

a lock-tripping failure must be shown to write exactly one login-lock: or address-lock: row in the same transaction as its own failure rows, and a failure that trips nothing none. A row written per refused request, or a lock row written apart from the failure, passes a test of the lock's length alone

the two-pages assertion must be made before page B sends any request: B holds no key, no decrypted name or figure and no typed name, every dialog is closed and the card is in Replaced elsewhere, all from the channel message alone. A test that lets B send a request first passes through the Conflict path and never shows the channel works

with the channel stubbed so no message arrives, B's save must answer vault-replaced, B must show Replaced elsewhere and post its epoch, the vault's records afterwards must be exactly the restored set, and the Conflict must never reach the holding form's version-reload path. A handler that treats it as a lost version check reloads the record and keeps B open on a vault that no longer exists

the coming-back-into-view page must send exactly one GET /api/records?type=profile and nothing else, while hidden it must send nothing and stay drawn, and its session row must still exist afterwards. A page that closes on hiding, or one that revokes the session, passes the visible half

sign-in must be shown to compare the epoch it returns against the one the page held, on an unlock of a live session and on a sign-in from the session-ran-out card, and to show no notice after a sign-out then sign-in, or a reload then sign-in, following a restore. Showing the notice after every restore, or after none, passes one half of the list

the dropped-input wording must be asserted for a typed form, for a kept dialog with nothing typed in it (a kept dialog counts) and for nothing kept, on both the card and the dashboard notice, with the critical icon present only in the first two. A page that tests only the typed form passes all three wordings with one

a channel message must be shown to be ignored when it names an epoch the page does not hold, has any other shape, or arrives while the page holds no epoch, and every posted message must have replaced as its only key holding the replaced epoch. A message carrying the new epoch or a key hands the new epoch to every page of the browser

the epoch must be shown absent from localStorage and sessionStorage across the whole flow. The epoch survives a lock in page memory, and an implementation that keeps it in storage to survive the lock passes every functional test

the posted message must be asserted from the page that learned by Conflict or at sign-in, and absent from a page that learned by message. A page that re-posts on receiving makes every page on the channel post in a loop
